summary: Amina Ali Qassim says her family narrowly escaped their home on Yemen's Birim island before missiles destroyed it during the Saudi aerial bombardment. At dawn, they joined three other families in a boat carrying 25 people and endured a five-hour crossing to Djibouti. The government is temporarily housing them in an unfinished orphanage in Obock before they move to tents, while the United Nations expects thousands more refugees. Having lost nearly everything, Qassim is also unable to contact her two daughters trapped in Taiz and fears the lasting effects of the bombardment on her infant granddaughter.

Australian police arrested five men aged 18 or 19 in Melbourne on Saturday in a major counterterrorism operation, then released three while inquiries continued. Sevdet Besim, 18, was charged with conspiring to commit a terrorist act and denied bail, while a 19-year-old remained in custody without yet appearing in court. Authorities alleged that the suspects planned to attack police at an April 25 Anzac Day ceremony marking the centennial of the Gallipoli Campaign, with civilians also at risk. Federal Police acting deputy commissioner Neil Gaughan said evidence and other information suggested the alleged plot was inspired by ISIS. Police said the suspects were associates of Nadun Haider, an 18-year-old killed while stabbing police officers in September. Victoria Police stressed that the men acted as individuals and did not represent any religious, cultural or national group. Gaughan expressed concern about their youth and urged earlier community efforts to identify such behavior. Prime Minister Tony Abbott said about 100 Australians were fighting with terrorists in the Middle East and another 150 people in Australia supported them through financing and recruitment. He urged Australians to continue their normal lives and attend Anzac Day commemorations in large numbers. Police said the specific threat had been fully contained.

Hundreds of decomposed corpses were discovered in shallow graves and on the streets of Damasak after the town was freed from Boko Haram in a joint Nigerian-Chadian military operation; residents who participated in the exhumations put the figure at more than 400. The victims included men, women and children murdered by Boko Haram when they seized the area in November, said Abubakar Kyari, a senator-elect for the region.

ISIS claimed responsibility for a suicide car bomb attack Friday near the U.S. Consulate in the Kurdish Iraqi city of Irbil, according to several Twitter accounts linked to the terror group. At least four people were killed and 18 injured, police said; a separate official, B.G. Hazhar Ismail, said three civilians were killed and five others were injured. Security personnel fired at the car, which exploded but did not reach the consulate, a police official said. All U.S. Consulate personnel were safe and accounted for following the explosion, U.S. State Department spokeswoman Marie Harf said.

James Best, best known for his portrayal of bumbling sheriff Rosco P. Coltrane on TV's "The Dukes of Hazzard," died Monday after a brief illness at 88. Best died in hospice in Hickory, North Carolina, of complications from pneumonia, said Steve Latshaw, a longtime friend and Hollywood colleague. Although he'd been a busy actor for decades in theater and in Hollywood, Best didn't become famous until 1979, when "The Dukes of Hazzard's" cornpone charms began beaming into millions of American homes almost every Friday night. For seven seasons, Best's Rosco P. Coltrane chased the moonshine-running Duke boys back and forth across the back roads of fictitious Hazzard County, Georgia, although his "hot pursuit" usually ended with him crashing his patrol car. Among the most popular shows on TV in the early '80s, "The Dukes of Hazzard" ran until 1985 and spawned TV movies, an animated series and video games. Born Jewel Guy on July 26, 1926, in Powderly, Kentucky, Best was orphaned at 3 and adopted by Armen and Essa Best, who renamed him James and raised him in rural Indiana. Best served in the Army during World War II before launching his acting career. In the 1950s and 1960s, he accumulated scores of credits, playing a range of colorful supporting characters in such TV shows as "The Twilight Zone," "Bonanza," "The Andy Griffith Show" and "Gunsmoke." "I laughed and learned more from Jimmie in one hour than from anyone else in a whole year," co-star John Schneider, who played Bo Duke, said on Twitter.

Feidin Santana said another officer ordered him to stop filming after he witnessed North Charleston officer Michael Slager fatally shoot Walter Scott, who was unarmed and fleeing; Santana's recording led to Slager's dismissal and arrest on a murder charge. Santana said he never saw Scott grab the Taser or receive CPR, although the initial struggle was not recorded and police accounts differed.

The latest high-profile digital incursion, in December, attempted to steal data from South Korea's nuclear operator, including plant blueprints and personnel information. Codes used in the attack were said to be similar in pattern to those used by the North Koreans, South Korean authorities said.

Koch Industries' recent announcement that it will "ban the box" -- i.e., remove from its job applications the check-box that asks about convictions -- is a big step forward in the movement to break down barriers to employment for job-seekers with records. "Ban the box" doesn't prohibit background checks, it only postpones them until later in the hiring process. Two generations of the war on drugs, zero tolerance, and aggressive policing have left 70 million adults with arrest or conviction records that undermine their ability to be considered for jobs, even as the job market has grown steadily. Now it's time for President Obama to lead the way and embrace fair-chance hiring of people with records.

The migrant crisis that has suddenly drawn hundreds of journalists to Sicily has been brewing for years, but in the past 10 days, with as many as 1,600 deaths in the Mediterranean, suddenly minds are focused -- for now. The fall of Libyan leader Moammar Gadhafi's regime, which we reporters covered so avidly, was followed by chaos, which we in the news media largely neglected, focused as we journalists were on the next catastrophe, the Syrian civil war. In that chaos, the business of human trafficking has boomed. Aware of the tragedy underway, however, Italians are alarmed at the prospect that this year alone as many as a million migrants could arrive in Europe, according to one European Union official. That is certainly the case in the Sicilian port of Catania, where many migrants arrive. The city's mayor, Enzo Bianco, insists city residents bear no ill will toward the migrants, but says Catania, and Sicily cannot absorb the ever-growing numbers. The rest of Europe must help carry the burden. Two northern regions, Veneto and Valle d'Aosta, have declared they will no longer accept new migrants. Others, however, insist Italy must keep its doors open. But now, today, Italians are grappling to deal with the consequences of an array of old and new ills, ranging from failing states and failing economies to endemic corruption, hopeless poverty, oppression and injustice that no one state or group of states can solve without a gargantuan, expensive and politically daunting effort.
